title: Roger Rosengarten Joins The Lounge | Baltimore Ravens
text: Welcome into the lounge. I'm Ryan Mink here with Garrett Downing and we are thrilled to sit down with Ravens right tackle Roger Rosenarten. And Roger, there's a first for everything. And today you were the first player to ever meet us in the studio before we got here. That's how much of a friend of the lounge you are, right? We have friends of the lounge. You're such a friend that you met us here. >> Appreciate it. >> Absolutely. Yeah, I guess so. I I'll take that put that on a resume. Yeah. >> So exciting year three for you, Roger. Just uh what's what's your mindset as as you approach this year? >> Yeah. I know me and a lot of guys starting from a clean slate, you know, from ground up in terms of the offense and, you know, new teammates, new faces, seeing a lot of guys leave and new guys come in, you know. Um, but I think since we've started the offseason program and, you know, just kind of developing a good solid foundation with the offensive line room into a players and it's just gone up so far. So, I mean, uh, it's been it's been a really great good couple months and we've established a really good foundation and I'm looking to build off what I already had going from the first to second year to third year. So, >> yeah. Tell me if I'm if I'm on the money on this. Something that that I've noticed and a lot of fans have asked me about this. It just seems like the vibes are great. Like like at practice, at media day this week, it just seems like there's really good vibes for the team going into this season. >> 100%. >> Why do you think that is? And tell me a little bit about that. I mean, I think, you know, starting fresh, you know, it could be a little bit nerve-wracking, but when you have a good core, solid foundation of players like we got with Derek, Lamar, Z, um, Ronnie, you know, solid veteran guys like that and you could see the connection that they have with all the rest of, you know, the offensive staff, Coach Men, the defensive guys, and um, and you see the progression happen from the first day of football school to the last day of mini camp. It's been uh really smooth. It's been smoother than, you know, I think expected for a lot of people. So, um when you get that mix that with a lot of good players, I mean, vibes are going to be high. So, >> yeah. How do you look back on your season last year personally? You know, you had this great rookie season, take become a starter early on. Where do you feel like you took your game in year two? Yeah, you know, I think looking back on the whole season, you know, it wasn't anywhere near where as a team where you wanted to be, you know, with um all the losses and stuff and then as you look at the pitcher as a whole, you're like, man, that really sucked. And me looking at my game personally, I was like, man, what could I have done more? Um, you know, and I had a whole list of things, but looking back from my progression from my rookie year to my second year and now going in, I feel like I've only gone up upwards with that. You know, um, establishing a really strong foundation from a rookie year and building off that, you know, I feel like everything between my technique and certain alignments that and angles that I was looking to challenge, you know, from my second year, you know, I only kept on going forward. So I kept that snowball rolling and you know I think that showed within the numbers too. So yeah. >> So one thing I noticed is a when you were coming out of college you were a blocker that was always you had an aggressive mindset right like sometimes even in pass pro you would like to kind of jump the defender and >> and uh that's just seems like your mentality right and first OTAA's practice now we're not in pads and all that stuff so you can't be taking you can't be taking people to the ground but I saw that Literally the first snap I was like, "Oh, Roger Roger's getting after it this year." >> Yeah, absolutely. >> And uh and and I feel like your style of play fits what coach Led Dwayne Leadford really wants and that's speed off the ball, right? That's what Roger Rosen's known for. >> How do you see that fit? Yeah, you know, I think with Declan coming in and coach Led coming in, I mean, those two guys have formulated a really good plan for the offensive line, me specifically for my game and what my strong suits are. You know, I think it fits me to a tea. >> Um, so from that first day, what led emphasized was obviously speed off the ball and, you know, we're just we're running. You know, that's it's going to be one thing. We're going to play hard, play fast. So, um, I mean, it all falls in I think my strong suits of quality as a player. I think from our my first two years, I think I had a lot of strong qualities that fit in that offense, but I feel like it's going to shine even more in this one. So, >> coach Leadford has he was one of the the first hires that Jesse Mener had after getting the job and there's been a lot of excitement around what he is going to help bring to this group and we sat down with him and just loved his energy and and passion that he brings. But in terms of from a schematic standpoint and the way that he's coaching you guys, what do you think that he's going to help bring to this offensive line room? Yeah, I mean I think that mentality, the toughness, he established that from day one, you know, um we're going to be the first group that's going to finish down the field. Always be around the ball carry, you know, that's one thing he always says. And I think that's a good thing for offensive linement in general. You know, whenever there's a play that's finished, whether it's pass or run, if you're there to pick up your guy, you're always going to be there around the ball and finish. And so, um, you establish the speed off the ball and then you finish that throughout the play and, um, you know, good things are going to happen. So, I think coach Le has had a history of of guys playing with that kind of mentality and it's shown in the success that his players have had. >> Now, Roger, there's something with you like when I look at you and the foundation that you've built these first two seasons, then you add in this this this coaching staff and coach Leadford like we just talked about, like I look at what you could be able to do this year and I think that you could put yourself in the the echelon of the top right tackles in the game. Like I think that that is something that's certainly certainly feasible and uh could happen uh this year. What do you view uh as sort of either your goals or your your uh projections for what this year could look like for you? >> 100%. I mean I agree. I think building from my first and especially my second year, the growth I had there and you know receiving some of the small um you know accolades and some some things that you know my buddies have shown me on this or that or >> um you know I don't really pay too much too much attention to it but looking back on last season and the improvements I had within pass run you know and the things that offense alignment get scrutinized for I think that is going to put me in a really good spot from last year to this year is going to really build that foundational block to where I'm established myself as one of the most elite right tackles in the game and especially um we have a lot of good ones too. So when you talk tackles I want to be in that definitely that conversation and I've had a lot of good guys to learn from. So >> So your boys send you like your highlight clips of you putting people on their work. Yeah, usually I don't I mean I'm I'm not too big on social media, but um I'll have a buddy of mine probably Teddy or whoever uh send me like a text or something. So >> PF ranking, good PFF rankings. >> Yeah, something like that. So yeah, it's it's usually you don't want to hear the bad stuff. No one wants to hear the bad stuff. So um when you hear when you hear something good and positive like um like that stuff. So it feels good. Where where in your game do you feel like you are you have made and are still making maybe the biggest strides in your game? Yeah, I mean I especially think from my run game from my rookie year to my second year and now this year I think it's going to especially this year like the amount of strides I feel like I've made already within OTAAS to mini camp to the veteran mini camp like I could already tell from this system I it's going to definitely grow a lot more and especially pass I think pass protection it's a passing league now um it's such emphasis and um I think my pass protection can always get better. You know, I don't think anybody's going to be um the perfect pass protector. Um but uh I'd say especially run in and pass too. >> Yeah. What is it in in the run game where you feel like, oh yeah, that's clicking now? >> Yeah. I mean, it's just that foundation of quality of, you know, the schematics that coach Declan and um led run. You know, it's >> it's a lot of outside zone stuff. >> Yeah. A lot of wide zone, a lot. And it and it, you know, it sets it sets us up for a lot of different plays, especially with you having a explosive quarterback like Lamar. You know, defensive ends got to respect, you know, the boot, the outside zone with Derek. So, it's it gets them thinking, gets their feet moving and, you know, you mix that with speed off the ball and great technique, it's going to turn out well. So, >> how much do you like that is is getting out there on that edge and you're getting ready to pick somebody off, you know what I mean? >> Oh, yeah. Absolutely. I mean, even with the pin pull plays where they got me pulling out in space, you know, >> that's what I was wondering. Like there's been a couple of these plays this spring where I've seen you like you're into that second level where you would be going up against not only a linebacker, but you could be lined up against a safety situation is that I mean that that's got a kind of bright eyes in that situation. >> Yeah, it's all kind of it's all built off of that wide zone. You know, it's going to look like wide zone until we pitch it and go all the way outside. So, um, like I said, you know, that's kind of where my feel like my strong suit is is getting out in space and being being able to run and, um, matching dudes only within the D line, but especially in the secondary, especially those quicker guys. So, >> is that something the offensive linemen typically like to be out there and have that match up against? Obviously, you have the size advantage in those situations. Now, they're quicker guys, but is that something that most offensive like being able to get out in space and and deliver like that that knockout blow? >> Yeah. I mean, especially like if you have the athleticism to be out there and um can shake with those guys a little bit and you just get in front of them and obviously they don't have the weight or the strength to kind of compete in the trenches. So, if you get a good solid piece of contact on them, they're probably going to go flying. So, >> yeah. >> Yeah. >> Now, we we should have brought some champagne in here because we're celebrating Miles Garrett out of the AFC North, right? We could have toasted to that. >> We could have. Yes, absolutely. tell us about how you found out about the news and and what your initial reaction was. >> Um, let's see, it was last week OTAAS and we're going through and uh we finish a practice and then we're all going in and then there's like a small chatter with then going to the locker room and um I get done my postpractice routine and whatnot and starting to undress and get ready for the shower. Check my phone and the first the first text was Ronnie. Ronnie was Miles question mark. I was I was like what? and uh obviously checked the news and saw him go to LA. So um you know especially for guys in the north, especially those tackles, like all of us, I think we're did a little fist pump in the air. Um but uh whatever division that is over there, it's >> NFC West. >> NFC West. Yeah, with all those guys. >> So have fun seeing them twice a year, especially the left tackles. So yeah, >> I only see him five to 10 snaps a game. So, right, Ronnie Ronnie was the big Ronnie's the big champagne guy for for this one. So, >> uh, a couple last ones for me is just, uh, where do you feel like the offense is in turn in terms of learning Declan Doyle's system and do you feel like it it's still a lot of work to be done? Do you feel like the group has the foundation in place? Like, tell me where you guys feel as a unit in that regard. >> Yeah, I mean, Declan is he's such a smart mind within creating an offense to have explosive plays. That's one of our foundational pillars in our offense's explosive plays with the kind of players we have. I mean, it's a necessity. So, um, and the amount of details that he pays attention to that can't go unknown within the offensive line of the tight ends, receivers, running backs, you name it, quarterbacks, it's everything is detailed and it needs to be detailed throughout the whole play. And if it doesn't, then um things can go wrong. And that's where explicit plays can turn to only two yard gain. And those details that he harps on and he ex explains to the rest of the position coaches is I feel like part of the reason why I feel really confident about this offense. So >> I'm curious uh for your perspective on Ven Yuane, the rookie first round pick playing right next to you at right guard. What stood out about him so far? >> Man, V's come in and I mean he's he's been such a I think I think Coach M already mentioned it. He's he's already like you could already tell he's got the veteran mentality, you know, with kind of all the departures we've had in the offensive line room. You know, myself and Ronnie, I feel like have definitely kind of stepped up in that leadership, but you could tell like V coming in as a young guy like he is and kind of already that veteran mentality, you know, very detailed in his work. Um, you could definitely tell within the plays we're running, you could I've I couldn't tell if he's been in the league for 5 years or his first year. So, >> um, you know, the progressions he's made, the strides he's made along with the technique he has, and the god-given ability, it's it's it's exciting. So, you know, visa stud. >> How how much are the right tackle and right guard kind of joined at the hip? How much is teamwork between those two pieces? >> Oh, it's everything. I mean, it's everything within pass protection, run game, you know, and if one guy is off, then you know, the play is going to either go for 15 yards or minus five TFL, >> right? >> So, um, you know, V's come in, like I said, and it feels like I've been playing the guy for a couple years. it's he's come in our communication has been >> I feel like the best it's ever been and you know um he's he's he's going to be really good players so I feel like that connection between myself and him is is going to be really strong on the right side. >> So that was your champagne toast when they d when they drafted him you were >> I mean whoever whoever we got but especially like a a player like V and the mentality he has you know it's definitely um definitely makes my job a little bit easier. So >> yeah. Do you do you talk to him about what comes with starting as a rookie like you've lived that you've gone through that or do you feel like okay he as you just talked about he already seems like a veteran. Do you not talk about it? What's your approach on that? >> For sure. Yeah. I mean I give him I give him tips and tricks you know kind of things that I did and especially I was telling him about my my growth from offseason otaas to training camp. I feel like I made such a big stride there and I feel like he's already uh way far ahead of than where I was >> and uh so I'll give him tips and tricks there and especially he's he's he's always a great learner too. He's always asking questions um what my thought process is going into a play in a certain schematic we're running. So um yeah, he's he's and he's all ears too. It's also another great quality about V being a good offensive lineman. >> It's awesome. And last question for me, Roger, is, you know, last year, I think part of the struggles overall, you know, people were talking about the offensive line and whatnot. >> Just with this group now, you lose Tyler Lindbomb, you lose a Pro Bowl center, which is is tough, right? >> But where do you feel like this line is? How good do you think it's going to be this year with you add new O line coach, you know what I mean? Like >> John Simpson comes in. >> John Simpson comes in. Exactly. Like do you feel do you get the sense now in OTAA's like yeah this we're we're going to have a really strong o offensive line even though we lost to Pro Bowl center. >> Yeah for sure. I mean losing Tyler stung. I think I said last year if we lose him it's going to sting. So I mean I was at his I was at his wedding recently and >> um I was happy for him but I'm also I was I was a little bummed. >> I was I was a little bit but uh man I'm so happy for him though. A guy like him he he deserves it. He deserves every bit of it. So, um, you know, last year was, you know, not the year we wanted, especially up front. Um, and, you know, coming with the clean slate and you get a veteran guy like John who's already been here, >> who I used to watch film as a rookie of John of John killing dudes. So, I already know he has the mentality for it. And you mix that with a good scheme that kind of fits all of our all of our kind of play styles >> with V in there and you know Danny and Joe and Cory battling for that center job. You know I think it's going to be um a lot better. A lot better. And you know that expectation is going to be set high but I think we're willing to challenge it. So >> awesome. Well that's music to uh our ears. Can't wait to see it out there bud. Thanks for thanks for having me on. Appreciate it guys. >> You're listening to the Lounge Podcast. We are coming to you from the SeatGeek studio. Big shout out to Roger Rosarten, multi-time friend of the lounge, as you said, he's such a friend that he has a keys. He has the keys to the building. Uh he comes into the lounge whenever he wants. Beat us here. And uh it was good to sit down with him. And and like I said to him, like I wasn't just doing the classic like you're interviewing the guy, you got to you know, you know, gas him up by telling him he's going to be great. Like I really feel that way about him. Like I think he could when it's said and done this year. I think that he could be in the Pro Bowl conversation >> and I think that people could be looking at him saying like, "Wow, he's going to get a huge contract ultimately and he's one of the best right tackles in the game, >> right? He's going to be a guy that I think people are talking about, can the Ravens get an extension done with him. You'd love to lock him up long term." Roger Rosenard's a really, really good player. He's also been extremely durable, consistent. I mean, that's what you want from your tackles, right? Works hard. He's out there every single practice. I don't I can't remember Roger missing practice. Like he's everything that you want. Yeah. And so I and I agree with you. I think with his skill set, with this scheme that Declan and Coach Leadford are bringing in here, I think that it just all fits really well and it's going to allow Roger and and everybody on this offensive line to flourish. Well, I really I I mean, I've said this many times, like I I love coach Leadford and everything that I've seen from him, watching him in the practice field, like the energy that he brings, the attention to detail was something that's very consistent amongst everybody on this coaching staff. And so, I I love all those things. Also, you put a first round pick in Venga Yawan next to him who look, the Ravens made no bones about it when they drafted him. Like, he's going to be a starter right away. And the expectation is that this guy's going to be as his career progresses one of the best guards in football. That's the hope. That's the vision. >> It's no secret that Daniel Falle struggled at times last year. And I think that that can also impact the players around you, right? Including Roger. And I think that having Wena next to Roger will help Roger also take that next step. And Roger's going to help Wena take that step as he establishes himself early in his career. I think it's just the right side of the offensive line, I think, is really going to be very solidified. >> Yeah, I think the line overall is is going to be a strength. I mean, I I think it is. Are they going to sign a free agent who's still out there? We'll see. But I agree with you. I feel very strongly about four of the five pieces right now. Yeah. >> And I think I've been I've been encouraged by what I've seen in OTAAS and mandatory mini camp from the center competition. And I I think you're going to get a lot more information during training camp when the pads come on, the physicality ramps up. But I think right now from everything that I see on the O line, I like its direction. >> My gut tells me though the starting center is on the team right now. I know that some people wonder are is there a move still to be made, a trade, whatever. Like you just mentioned, my gut tells me the starting center is on this team currently >> uh for week one. >> Yeah, I think that could very well be the case. >> And and I think that this group overall is going to be a strong unit. I think it's gonna I think that this offense is going to be excellent and I think that the offensive line is going to be a driving force of that of that offense's excellence. >> The offensive line has such a trickle down effect. It it really does start there because >> I also think it it's was pretty clear last year that Lamar Jackson didn't feel comfortable be behind the offensive line. He was fading away too much and that led to some of his struggles last year. >> Well, I mean honestly it wasn't just a feel. He was banged up, you know, for much of the year. Right. And so I think when this offensive line plays at a higher level, Lamar's going to feel more comfortable. He's going to play at a higher level. Not to mention what it's going to do for the run game and all of those things like it really does start up front and and has that trickle down effect. So I'm excited about it. >> Yeah, no doubt. So uh as always, we love your questions. Send those into the lounge the lounge at ravens.n.net. We love uh getting those questions. So make sure you send us those emails. Thank you so much for watching and listening. And we will be back with you again soon.

title: Trenton Simpson Could Unlock the Ravens Defense
text: You know, last year it just wasn't there. I think we've talked about this. I think he had no sacks for the first time in his career. He had no interceptions for the first time in his career. I think it was five tackles for losses and three of them were in that week two game against Cleveland. Three of them may have been in one half. Uh so, the rest of the 15 games he only had two tackles for losses. Um they need him to play much better and I think Roquan knows that. >> I'm trying to find the quote right now from Trenton Simpson cuz I think it's a really interesting point. He had a quote last I think it was last week where he was talking about being put in a different role um in this defense compared to his Clemson days. And reminds me a little bit if you guys want a comparison for someone from the Chargers that I think if you want to look for that like-for-like role, could actually be a really fun film piece to do. Um Henley, the linebacker they had last year. Undersized guy, but someone that he moved all over the field, used him as a blitzer, and he actually racked up 16 pressures last year and had multiple games uh with multiple pressures. And that's really what I think Trenton Simpson's role is going to be in this defense is that type of Henley role who's the linebacker for the Chargers last year. So, >> I've got that quote, by the way. >> You do got it. Okay. >> Of course he does. Bobby is all over this. >> The OG in the Hall of Fame, Cliff Brown, did a profile on Baltimore Ravens >> That's what it was. >> Yes. >> recently. Yeah. And I'll read part of the transcription here. My mentality in year four is great. My maturity, understanding, and preparation with everything is better. How to lift weights, how to eat, and take care of my body. I know it's showing because I feel so much faster. I feel like I'm ahead out there. Um he also wrote, let me get to the Clemson part. That's what I did at Clemson a lot. Uh having a bigger role and impact as a pass rusher. Moved around, came off the edge. I came from college really as a stand-up defensive end who moved. I always loved to spy the quarterback. The more versatile you are being on on edge, in the box, wherever can help a defense. I need to know all the spots. We're going to play quarterbacks who scramble. I believe I'm the guy on this team who can go get any quarterback. As long as I show that to the coaches and they gain that trust in me, I'll be ready to roll. Guys, we've seen flashes >> Yeah. >> of that at times when he's knifing through defense Is there anybody more athletic than this guy pound-for-pound on the team? >> I don't know. >> He'd be up there. >> Um but that that is one thing that I will say, you know, it's No one's been harder on Zach Orr than me. But one thing I will say about Zach Orr is when he was trying to make adjustments to get a pass rush going last year, and we talked about this quite a bit during the season, he had that package where they would, you know, walk Roquan up to the line, walk Trenton up to the line, and Trenton spied a lot. I think that's one of the very positive things that Orr did last year was trying to limit the quarterback scrambles with those delayed blitzes from a you know, like a blitz bluff alignment. And so, we've already kind of seen Trenton Simpson do it in a Ravens uniform. I know a lot of people just kind of think we played, you know, cover two, Tampa two, you know, cover six. But on third down, he liked to go to that type of look and get Simpson involved. So, I think that's something that he has experience doing and put him more in that role that you would have expected when he was at Clemson. So, I think the big thing is doing it more on a down-to-down basis so it's not so predictive or so predictable on third down. >> And look, they didn't add an They didn't add an inside linebacker this year. Not not I mean, signed a couple undrafted >> Not even a special teamer, which was insane. >> I know. There was a guy out there today, um There's a couple tryout guys out there today. Woods, uh Maryland kid, Baltimore kid, who played at University of Maryland. Josh Woods, I think his name is. He looked to be out there as a tryout player. He's been a linebacker and a special teams player throughout kind of at a couple different stops. Um but yeah, Bobby's right. I mean, they still have What is it What is the Fred Jones Jr. Um, is still on the roster, but >> Jay Rae Lewis Higgins. >> Yeah, Higgins was there. He's out there. Um, you would think if they were concerned about the position, uh, if they were concerned about Teddy Bridgewater's, um, you know, knee and his ability to respond, you would think they would have made that position a bit of more of a priority, but they didn't.

text: Coach Bennett good at his job. >> Oh man, Edgar has a a way about him as a as a person and as a coach that is extremely comforting in a way. He's very much calm, cool, collected. And um we're going away on uh Friday. I'm taking him overseas to go golf and we're going to do our uh our golf trip. So, we'll be together for Father's Day. And um you know, having him around here every day. He's got a locker in in the in the coach's locker room. And uh it's great having him here. Uh it's good for me, but it's also cool for our staff, our players that, you know, they all kind of uh connect with them in their own way. Grant Udinsky when you guys drafted Borcature said he was gonna change the offense. Is it easier to establish the culture or maintain the culture? >> That's a good one. >> Um, I think establishing is definitely a little easier, I think. Um, because look, they're very ready to hear something different, right? when you've lost or or coming off a tough year, they're eager. Their eyes are bright. They're they're, you know, they want to hear what you got to say because like, hey, man, this is this is what we got. This is what we have to go. And I think that was probably a little easier than sustaining it, right? Especially once we get to a point where maybe in a few years where you're, you know, other guys are moving on that have been in the locker room that know the culture and have the standards. We were very fortunate to be able to bring back a lot of those guys this year. And so, um, I Ross Massie was telling me, you know, out there on the grass that he's like, man, I told my wife this weekend that this is the closest team, you know, I've been around in a in my life. So, it's pretty cool to hear that and to see it come to life. Um, but I think sustaining it is is the challenge. sustaining your culture because now all right what happens if we you know we start lose some games and now you start looking at well man maybe that wasn't right maybe we aren't doing the right things but no we are you just stay the course process drives the results but man we can get caught up in those results pretty quickly and I think that's when it goes downhill this being a copycat league especially on defense have you looked at defenses this offseason what's the next trend after shell coverage >> I think um multiplicity in diversity within jobs and responsibilities on the defensive side. Different jobs, roles, responsibilities because now it allows you to have different packages, develop players because you're getting them on the grass a little bit earlier. I think there's just so many different things that we can do that'll open up our offense to where we're not predictable.

title: Comeback season for Texans' Tank Dell: What to know, interviews & more
text: Hey guys, Aaron Wilson. Tank Dell. The comeback continues and some really encouraging signs from the former University of Houston standout. Not only what we saw on the field, but his words. I had a chance to have a great conversation with him this weekend in Friendswood at Dick's House of Sports Fanatics event and Tank told me, "I'll be ready for training camp." So they ramped up his activity during the mini camp as we reported told you that he would. So he was able to take part in some drills. He seemed to have, you know, while maybe a little bit less explosive and dynamic, he didn't really seem like he was trying to cut it loose either. I saw someone that had a certain bounce in his step, caught the football with confidence, and even participated in a couple drills catching passes. He said that meant the world to him to be out there. camaraderie to be out there with Nico Collins to catch passes from his best friend CJ Strad. So truly inspirational thing to see from Tank Dell. I've known Tank for several years. I first met him when he was at the University of Houston and I was given some advice. You should head over across town and do a story on him. He's going to be in his final year of eligibility. He's going to do some special things. So I went over there and what I found was someone that just really refreshing, someone that loves football for the love of the game. And I think he'd play this game for free if he had to. And you think about Tank and what he's been through. Were Were you wowed like physically? It's much more of like a a strength thing that I think I I saw from him in the back shoulders and the slants than like he is exploding by everyone. It was a B+ A minus type little stretch here >> which you and I would kill for back in the day for the record. That's his game in a nutshell. And it's and it's for him to be to continue to be the receiver that he's been. Uh, and whether you're talking about the last two years when some of the numbers came down or what happened prior, which was pretty electric, he's still going to have to win that way. That's how he's going to have to win. So, what we did see in these few days of of competitive play was that's what he does. He still does that and that's what he's going to have to do going forward. And I you know, we can talk about the knee and whether you whatever. >> I don't really want to talk. >> Yeah. No, and I'm just saying that like obviously if if that goes south then we're talking about a different player. And you had some great stats about this the last time that we talked because those are the lowhanging fruit, the easy stuff where we're just watching this passing offense. Like I think Hunter Henry might have the fewest yards after the catch in the entire league. I understand he's more of a statues tight end, but the point is, aside from Bob Douglas, who they only trusted to play 26% of the snaps, there weren't guys who were catching and going, he is someone that in motion can get yards after the catch. When tackled, can shake it and get yards after the catch. He didn't have a chance to do that a whole lot this week. I'm excited to see it next time. All right, five minutes is up. Christian Gonzalez, you and I differed on this on Tuesday in like a pretty big way. So, I've sort of already said what I think about this or how I framed it in my head. You tell me why I'm being optimistic about him playing and doing more than I expected this week. >> Yeah, I didn't really think he did very much at all. I And because nothing was ever done at a full speed like when he was in there and I don't even think there were competitive periods. It was just very low-key. I I I think that this whole thing has baffled me a little bit, Andrew, because I think it's one of the um more pressing stories in the league. I mean, everybody looks at quarterback and, you know, contracts with quarterbacks and that's that's the driver. But there's two really good quarterbacks and he and Devin Witherspoon. Witherspoon went through everything. He did the voluntary stuff. He did the OTAAS. He did mandatory. He went through it two weeks ago was the last report I saw in his contract and they and it said they weren't close and yet he's going through everything. Christian chose to stay away. Personal decision. He said he stays away, not involved. When he comes back, I mostly saw him with a helmet not even in his hand. The helmet was on the ground. And therefore, it's like, well, I'm here because I'm not going to get fined because that's stupid. Why am I going to give you my money? But I'm not really going to go out of my way to do too much. >> So, what I saw, and correct me if I'm wrong, was a guy who participated in every drill and every period except the live 11on1s. I about participating and then doing it to your ability are two different things. I think it was, you know, obviously Wednesday was a walkthrough and a half speed day anyway, but I thought Tuesday he was doing a lot of half-speed stuff when when other people weren't doing half speed stuff. And I don't think it was a making a point to the coaches like I can just do whatever I want. I just think like I'm protecting myself. I'm here. I told you I'd be here. I'm not getting fined, but I'm also not going to hit break neck speed. I don't know that he hit top speed at any point in three days. >> They had that drill where they'll start in one corner of the field and players shoot out like 10 or 12 across in a way that almost if they were connected like they could carry a parachute and that they go out all in these different directions and cover almost like 90 degrees worth of space, right? And they're all just sprinting. They're just sprinting in different directions. He was sprinting for that period. So like he did hit top speed. I think it's hard because some of these drills, right, are just so elementary and they're the same thing they do before every practice is work on fundamentals and it's work on technique and certain different things. So like there's an element of that that's just you are literally going through the motions. You can have focus but it looks laxidasical because you're just doing it for the thousands and 78th time. To me, I was open to anything with Christian Gonzalez and that was a hold in where he suits up and sits down for three days and does nothing. So maybe my expectations were too low for this. I think it's fair to say that this seemed to be like a negotiated part and Vel said that maybe it was less than I don't have the reporting on this, but for him to do at least be in every drill and the seven on seven stuff when they were installing he was there. That's much more of a mental focus than it is a physical one. Like he was engaged it looked like mentally even if it was half speed because that's kind of the nature of threequarters of the drill. >> Yeah. I don't think that's to go back to your original point actually as I'm I'm thinking this through. I thought he wouldn't do anything. Like I I I was with you. My my expectation was he was going to show up and he was going to stand there in shorts and a t-shirt. He wasn't even going to have his helmet and he wasn't going to do anything. So if you're looking for that the glass is half full, then that's clearly glasses half full because my expectation was at the very bottom of the of this process. I do wonder too if the relationship between coacher and player improved to the point where as Mike said they've had these conversations and they were good conversations wouldn't tell us what those conversations were that Mike was like hey can you at least be mentally engaged here in the process you know I don't control this whole contract thing your agent Elliot whoever they're all dealing with that when I you got to be here so when you're going to be here can you make sure that you're at least zoned in for when you're here and you're locked on what we're trying to do and that the respect between the two men is enough that Christian's like, "Okay, I I can do that for you, coach." And so, you know, I guess if again, if you're looking glass half full, maybe that's the way I would look at it. >> Yeah. All right. This is the more interesting part to me is what happens next. Um, and I have a lot to run through you here, but I don't want to take up the rest of our time doing this because we got to talk about Drake May. The name Sauce Gardner has come to mind a lot in the last 24 hours, and it's been for a couple of reasons. Number one, two years ago, Sas Gardner, former first round pick, elite corner, looking for an extension, got his days before Jets training camp. I understand in the for you know, forefront here, the Jets and Patriots are worlds apart. And the Jets then >> when they traded Sus Gardner just over a year later, we're rebuilding. You don't have to point out the differences in the situation, but hear me out. So, they signed him to an extension right before training camp. I think that's illustrative of the timing the Patriots would like to have and that your one of your best players is on board. He's extended. You don't have to think about this. No distraction, no holding, no wondering. He's just on the field healthy and gets to be available for week one in a way that he wasn't last year and really wasn't himself until mid-season because he was nursing an injury he sustained in training camp. Number two is when they did trade him in November, he got two first round picks in return. And if I'm the Patriots and I go, "Okay, we did not sign him to an extension right before training camp. We have to go on to plan B." What I would consider is this. Giving a little bit of ground in negotiations, understanding that if you were the Patriots, who were dead last in cash spending from 2014 to 2023, according to ESPN, and you just signed AJ Brown to $29 million, making him the highest paid player in this team, and third highest paid Patriots player ever for a single season. Drake May is going to get a contract now that might be $70 million per year when he gets extended, presumably next spring. And now a third premium player at a premium position is going to sign this big extension. Even if you don't like the number or find it palatable, a you keep him under contract long term to keep him for this season when clearly you're going for this is a Super Bowl. >> And you keep him happy. Number two, you keep him with the idea of when we sign Drake to that contract and an ownership group that again, I would pay him, they should pay him. This is all worth it. this is what you are a billionaire with a sports team for to pay the best players to have them on your team and to go win games and championships. But if they're unwilling to do that or don't find that they can, you can recoup the 2028 first round pick that you lost in the AJ Brown trade presumably because just as Drake May will be extended in 2027. AJ Brown has $4 million guaranteed to him next year. So, he's going to need an extension. And we could talk about how Christian Gonzalez is only going to be turning 24 soon. And again, freak athlete entering his prime. The thing is the corner position of quarterback, pass rusher, offensive tackle, and receiver. They're other premium spots. Corner is the least predictive and sticky and stable year-to-year, meaning it's harder to predict what they're going to do. We can get into the reasons why. Those are just the facts. Corners are more of a roller coaster than any of the other spots. So, even if AJ is older, Drake May is a separate conversation. There's a world in which they can lose the negotiation and still get what they want. And I'm not saying they should do this. I just think it's something to keep in mind and on the table where best case scenario, they sign him and keep him. But to me, even if he gets that extension, his future is not guaranteed in here because the crafts are going to have to do something that they just have not done. Paid three premium players at top of the market prices for long-term deals all within the next 12 months. And it's just something I'm keeping in mind like especially in light of the Mahomes contract. So whether this happens or not like again I hope they sign them. I hope they extend Brown in May and all this is easy. But we know it's often not when it comes to contract negotiations. Am I getting too ahead of myself? Well, and an addendum to that as well is that as we're talking about, clearly they're all in for this season. Um, just based on how they've constructed their roster, but at the end of the season, it's Hunter Henry, it's Mike and Wenu. There's a number of important players reaching different stages of their careers who are going to be up for new contracts. And so, you're either replacing them with in-house, which again, we'll see how things develop over the course of the year. I can't tell you if they have those guys here or not. But right now, I would say probably not. Uh, and we'll again, we'll see how the year plays out. So, there's going to be positions that you're going to have to spend some money on or invest draft capital in. Um, my second point was I don't think you're get I don't know where you were talking about recapping recouping the 2028 first. Do you think you're going to get two first round picks? >> If you were to put Christian Gonzalez up for market, do you think you get two first round picks? I don't think so. >> I think I think that that deal for Indianapolis went so sideways and it was a physical thing more than anything. And again, I applaud them for doing it because I they were at the time when they made that trade, they were probably the best team in the AFC. And then he's hurt. >> Daniel Jones blows out his Achilles. Yeah. I mean, I they were Dude, they were they were balling. Um >> I just don't think you're going to get that. I think I think any GM will look at that and go, "Man, you said it's a volatile position in terms of performance. You can't really quite predict it. Do I really want to give up two first round picks and then have it happen to me? What just happened to the Colts?" And now I'm like, "Oh, well, kind of have to, I don't know, rebuild, but we're kind of stuck in this middle place." And we don't have that first round pick. We don't have that second first round pick. I think you get one for him. I don't think you're getting two. I I think you would definitely at a minimum get a a first and then a day two pick at worst. I mean, I just the market's been set like Howie Roseman was going about pointing to the Jaylen Wadd deal and um I can't remember some of the recent trades that were brought up. Breer had the report, but the point is like look, the market is what the market is. And there are certain deals that you're right, there are outliers that every other GM goes, hey, I know Deshun Watson got $230 million guaranteed. all of it, the whole deal. We're not doing that. And the only quarterback to surpass that since then happened three, four years ago is Patrick Mahomes just a couple of days ago. Point is, he's younger than than Sauce was, I think, when he signed that or got traded. Um, look, we are going down the line. The point is like the front office is mapping these things out and having contingency plans as you and I speak and already has them in place. If this, then we do that. If that, then we're going to have to do this. And the conversations with ownership, which I don't like. I think the spending talk is overrated just because of the way Bill operated and that was the biggest variable in how the Patriots spent their money. Um, but right now it's a lot of cash on the way out and particularly with the signing bonus that Christian Gonzalez would get and then Drake May would get signed them, pay them all. I just think this is something to keep in mind where even if he does get the extension, he might not be guaranteed to be here for long given what they're going to try to at least recoup which presumably would be some 2028 draft capital. Well, so so to me, they're obviously going to pay May, unless that went completely sideways. >> Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. >> And because they gave up the first round pick for AJ Brown, unless that goes sideways, they're going to pay him at least for one more year. So that raises the question, will they pay that next guy, Christian Gonzalez, will they pay him top of the market money at the quarterback position and have three players who are going to be at or near the top of the position in terms of money? And while I will agree with you that Bill liked to do things a certain way and like to win negotiations and all that, ownership also played a hand in that. And so until they do it, Andrew >> Yeah. Yeah. >> I'm not going to believe they're going to do it. That's kind of where I stand. >> But they absolutely should. >> You do the deal and the cap pain is not going to hit right away with Gonzalez this year. So like that's not a consideration. You also have time, let's say it happens in July to reshape your roster in terms of drafting a corner maybe on day one or day two of next year, signing extra pass rushers to like be prepare yourself to brace for his eventual departure if if if you do trade him, which again we're getting ahead of ourselves, but like look, they have to juggle this. The money, the cash, the cap, um the players, the investment, they're all in. Hopefully this goes well. Just something to keep in mind. We have one minute for Drake May. Um [laughter] >> I can give you five. >> Okay. All right. He was 27 of 40 over two practices. Take that for whatever you like, whatever you don't. Two sacks was my favorite number from him um over these two practices. Seven touchdowns on 20 drop backs on Thursday. I've talked a lot about his control at the line of scrimmage or writing about it for Sunday. They're giving him new tools. Some of them are old that Josh just didn't have installed or covered um last year. Some of them are new as they always introduce things into the offense. What interests you most about Drake May and or what is most important about what you saw this week? >> I think I mentioned off the top. I just love the amount of control. I think it's the little things too for me watching him interact with his teammates. Last year we know the focus non-stop from Vrabel was like, "Why are you standing over here? Go talk." Every time they posted a clip on patriots.com on Twitter, it was Vrabel telling him to go talk to his teammates. Go celebrate with your teammates. And I heard Vable say that a few times. I don't think it was ever directed at Drake during the course of these three days. Like I think he was front and center. He was involved in all that stuff. He even jawed a little bit with some of the defensive guys. Not quite Tom Brady against Vrabel the player or Rodney Harrison the player as they did uh famously back in the early 2000s, but like it just he's really comfortable in his own skin. He's really comfortable with the offense. I think he's comfortable with what they're asking. I I think he's so comfortable as as Josh told us like you know he's asking a lot of questions of him and bringing up different points and like this is all part of the maturation of what you believe is the franchise quarterback and I saw nothing that would uh lower my level of confidence in the player taking yet another step this year even though as we know based on what happened last year and the numbers he put up etc and the run they went on that's going to be hard to do. I still feel pretty confident that he's going to be able to do it. >> I do too. And this next part sounds maybe ridiculous for the guy who had the most accurate season in the NextGen stats era going back to 2018. I think this receiving court is even better suited for his throwing style and his game and his ability to fit balls into tight windows because he he's much more of a downfield jump ball, bigger receiver type of guy. Like yes, of course he played with he plays with Pop Douglas and played with Stefon Digs. I just think AJ Brown is a guy who wins more on those back shoulders, wins physically. Like Romeo Dobs's one touchdown was a jump ball. Dobs would have had another if Kevin Byer hadn't stripped it down. Like that's what May is and does best. I think this is not only just oh they improved his receiving core they got him type of weapons which was you know I I could say in the theoretical when these moves happened or not when I was on paternity leave but now that I've seen it I just go okay this fits in a way the same way that all of these jitter bugs over the middle fit Brady with that just elite alltime accuracy within 10 yards of the line of scrimmage because of his ability just to pinpoint and pew pew pew the ball where he wanted and Brady could rip it. Obviously this is not to pick one or the other. It's just to say that I think, you know, Hunter Henry and AJ Brown leading in touchdowns when they spent so much time in the red zone was not an accident. These are go get it back shoulder top of the ladder type of throws and that's the stuff that he excels at. So, I'm I'm excited. The other stuff, you know, again, talk about theoretical like his answers and solutions and checks. He'll just need to continue to get reps against defenses like Seattle's that we're going to see week one. Um, but I'm encouraged by the comments and what I've also seen by him doing that at break neck game break neck gameplay speed problem solving because that really is the next step and the next level for him and what they're going to need as defenses continue to get better against him and and disguise. >> Yeah. Yeah. And I think you and I are writing about something along the similar lines for this weekend. And I I just I love the way they challenged him. Like we hear all the time and you've been covering this for a long time. I've been covering it for a long time that this time is the teaching time and we you know people evaluate this, evaluate that and it's like well you know they are to a degree but mostly it's just teaching and making sure guys are playing fast and in the right place and understand the concepts and everything. We're going to get you the line of scrimmage, but I ain't giving you a play. And now the the the clock is down to 18 seconds and you got to read the defense. You got to get your guys lined up. You got to realize what personnel you have on the field, too. Like all these different things. And you got to spit out that play and you have to attack the weakness. And I think that is brilliant. Probably too strong of a word, but I I just I love that they're challenging him mentally at this time of year. Not like, "Hey, we're we're taking the next step now, man. You know the language. We're going to open up a little bit more to you now and then if you handle that, we're going to throw a little bit more and a little bit more like till you show that you can't handle it." And he's showing so far that he can handle it. So, I just love that aspect of it. And, you know, Josh was a whipping boy after the Super Bowl obviously. Um, people didn't think he gave him the right answers. Where's screen pass? Well, they couldn't run screens all year, but whatever. you know, be as it may, you want to you want to actually follow the facts and the numbers of the whole thing. But I think having him back for a second year and for them to be able to expand on the relationship is massive for the offense and combine that with, as you said, getting targets that he's comfortable with. As he told us, I I threw to my brothers, we're all like six foot seven. >> Seven. But like he is comfortable. I I think we made the point early in the year like with Pop like that he's not super comfortable throwing it to Pop or at least he wasn't last year and I think part of it was just the size. He wasn't totally adjusted to that type of receiver and now that I think their chemistry has built a little bit here over the course of the season last season and now into the spring but like yeah it all sort of fits what the quarterback wants but also doing it within the framework of how Mike wants to play and how Josh wants to call a game. Yeah, coming together. Uh, it was a fun, fierce, hotly contested, I think is the way I described it. Practice on Thursday. This is a pretty cool, calm episode for the two of us. So, >> enjoy the break. Uh, I'm not going to bug you for at least like six weeks. How about that? >> Six whole weeks. >> I'm gonna be sad. What am I going to do? >> That's a great question. Hopefully watch more NBA Finals and World Cup uh with prize picks in your hand. All right. You have a haircut. You have to go jealous. And uh anyway, we will reconvene close to the start of training camp. Pleasure as always and I'll chat with you soon. >> See you.

text: I knew there would be something more with Brendan Sorsby, the NCAA, and Texas Tech and now the Big 12. That was today's development. Actually, two developments. The NCAA's filed its appeal of the ruling that came down last Monday requesting an expedited briefing schedule with the goal of resolving the case before the start of college football season. That doesn't really help Sorsby. He needs it to be resolved by next Monday, June 22, because that's the deadline for entering the supplemental draft. More on that in a minute. Separately, and there was some huffing and puffing in both directions last week between the Big 12 and Texas Tech over whether the Big 12 is able to sanction Texas Tech for playing Sorsby under conference bylaws. The victory that Sorsby secured last Monday only applies to NCA bylaws. So the argument is we as a conference can still do something if Texas Tech puts this player on the field who has violated repeatedly the NCAA gambling rules. And one of the things mentioned in this new lawsuit and I mentioned it last week and you know we got to take a step back from the addiction that Brendan Sorsby suffers from and we have to acknowledge the behavior preceded the addiction and the behavior at the root of this involves gambling when he was under the age of 21 which isn't legal in Ohio where this got started. It's not legal anywhere that anyone can gamble under the age of 21. And a lot of the gambling he did happened when he was under 21. And a lot of the gambling he did happened through third parties, which is a separate violation. So that's part of what the Big 12 is going to harp on as it attempts to secure the ability to sanction Sorsby indirectly by sanctioning Texas Tech. And what they've done, they filed a lawsuit in federal court in Dallas to try to secure the ability to potentially sanction Texas Tech if enough of the members of the Big 12 vote to do so. They haven't decided to do it yet, but because of the back and forth last week, you had Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton basically saying, "Bring it on." You have the Big 12 at the urging of the Oklahoma Attorney General thinking about what it's going to do. And I I think that Sorsby's camp would admit today that they probably made a mistake by not immediately filing an amended complaint in the Leach County lawsuit against the Big 12 to force them to respect the ruling that keeps Sorsby eligible despite the alleged violation of the NCA gambling policy. Obviously, it was violated. The question is whether or not, and this is where it gets into the nuances of the case that aren't in the four-page ruling that was issued last week. That's the biggest problem I have with it. We don't have enough to really understand why the judge worked his way through the maze and came to the conclusion that Sorsb is eligible given the fact that he admits that he violated the gambling policy repeatedly. So, you know, sometimes you get in a situation where there's a race to the courthouse and and we don't know whether or not Sorsby's lawyers were in the process of putting something together that would have attacked the Big 12 in the existing case. That would have been the better move. You've got a favorable judge state court level. You've already gotten a win. You're going back into court and you're saying, "Hey, stop the Big 12 from doing an end run around the ruling that's already on the books." Instead, you got the Big 12 going into federal court in Dallas and possibly coming away with a ruling that allows the conference to sanction Texas Tech if they play Sorsby in a game. So, they are doing in a roundabout way what the NCA can't do. And there's probably some regret from Sorsb side that they didn't think more broadly about this when attacking the NCAA's decision and they maybe should have made it broad enough so that the Big 12 wouldn't be able to take action. But you know what? This is unprecedented. So the next time that someone's in this situation, if there is a next time, I guarantee you the NCA and the conference will be joined in the lawsuit. Even if the conference hasn't made it clear that it's going to do anything, you want to seal off any avenues for preventing Brendan Sorsby from playing. That's what that initial lawsuit was about. In a good way. the the NCAA's antitrust violations were so prevalent that not only did they refuse to pay the players, they refused to let the players make any money off of their name, image, and likeness. That's what started all this. the Ed Oandon lawsuit against EA Sports, the one that took away college football from the EA Sports library because they were using the names, images, likenesses, and maybe not the names, but at a minimum when you when you played the game, you knew who you were playing with because it was the same shape, size, number, position. And what I try to do with these legal concepts, because I did practice for 19 years, and I feel like I need to say that from time to time because folks will say, "What the hell do you know? title: ESPN’s Mike Breen Talks New York Knicks’ NBA Championship with Rich Eisen | Full Interview
text: And joining us right now is a long-time voice of the Knicks and the NBA Finals, uh fresh off of his 21st NBA Finals in a row that he has called for ESPN and ABC. Um a friend, Mike Breen, is here on the program. Good to see you, Mike. How are you? >> Hello. Hello, Rich. How are you, bud? >> I'm doing great. I mean, those scenes I mean, you're you're a New Yorker, you're a Fordham guy. Like seeing those scenes, like come on, right? Like this is crazy. >> I've never seen anything like it. And you know, you you talked about the text that your fan uh or your friend sent. You know, the emotion of caring is um it's an amazing thing and the way sports fans care, I don't know if you've ever seen Roger Angell, a great writer. He he wrote a little essay on what it means to be a fan and I anybody who's ever been a sports fan needs to look it up. It's easy to find. And you know, the this whole idea of caring so much about something that you become this irrational person in so many ways and you spend all your time and all your all your money and you know, all your emotion comes pouring out and it hurts so badly when they lose, but then when an event happens for Nick fans like happened the other night, um the joy is just it's overwhelming and I saw it at the arena. I saw it in those videos that that you just had and it's just a beautiful thing. Um it's it's you know, we keep saying that sports is the great unifier. My son, Matt, who watched the he's 29. He watched the game with some friends at at one of their apartments in the city and then afterwards the game they went out and he said in about a three walk block three block walk, he said, "Dad, I hugged like 80 strangers." >> [laughter] >> And then when does that ever happen in New York? >> Hey, man, I I you know, my wife printed out uh Stevie Nicks t-shirts, you know, um the one that Taylor Swift wore the other day. So, I was I was wearing walking the dog with her yesterday in Los Angeles and there was a guy with a Knicks hat walking the other way and he's like, "How great is life?" You know, like we shared this moment in a small street in Los Angeles on on Sunday. And you know, to your point, Mike Green by the way has joined us here. Our radio audience has just returned. The word fan is the root for the word fanatic. You know, like that is it. That's that's what we're describing here. And you've had a front row seat quite literally for all of these years. Um, what do you think this championship for the Knicks means? >> It's it's one of the great great moments in New York sports history for a number of reasons. First and foremost New York has always been a basketball town. I mean, I've lived in New York my whole life and we all love football, we all love basketball. I'm not saying one's more important than the other in terms of the fans, but there's just something something about the city game being basketball. So, that's number one. Number two, it's it's a team that pretty much the entire city gets behind. And it's a team that has struggled for so long. But the fans never went away even in the rough years. And there were many rough years as we all know. So, to go from that and stick with them through thick and through thin and see not only a team that have success but a team that that is such representative of the city and the kind of people that you want they're they're such high character individuals. They're all about the team, the way they carry themselves. Uh, that's a big part of it as well. And then when you have your star player be the kind of young man that Jalen Brunson is from a player to his toughness uh, to his will of never giving up uh, to overcoming all the yeah, he's good but stuff. Um, that's an important factor as well. And you know, I I I said this the other day and it might sound a little corny, but so Brunson has all these these different characteristics that that you want in your star player, that you want in your franchise player. One that that sometimes goes underrated, he's extremely coachable. Um even at this level, he's extremely coachable and that's huge for a team to come together because if if the rest of the team sees, okay, this guy's taking some some uh guff from the coach and and the coach gets on him, not just the head coach, but of course the assistant, namely one Rick Brunson, then then we can do it, too. So, you put it [snorts] all together and it just it becomes something really magical. Um and that's that's what we always hope for. That's the long long-term dream when we start rooting for a team to have a team like this. >> Yeah, I mean and again, being such a fan that I am, Mike, I've spent, you know, probably too much time on my phone in the last 36 hours just scrolling for any all of it, just soaking all of it in. I mean, I your your essay after the game five was perfect. Spot on. It was beautiful. I took that in. I took in the entire Inside the NBA postgame because the number of times I've watched those guys on TNT rightfully disparage the Knicks and their plans and their results, just to take that all in, right? I mean, soaking it all in. The one video that keeps on popping up is Rick Brunson, I believe in the Atlanta series down two games to one, um just having a moment with um with Jalen where he's clearly telling him whatever Jalen's upset about or complaining about to knock it off. >> Right. >> And and it's I do remember when Rick Brunson was hired or brought on and kept on, uh you know, the narrative was they're coddling >> [snorts] >> Jalen Brunson. And it's the exact opposite, [laughter] right? So, what would you say what what's your favorite Jalen Brunson story, Mike? What is that? >> It's It's to to have a an individual one. He was devastated. Like devastated. And and that's really who he is. It's you know, everybody loves to win but how many are truly devastated um when they lose like that and that made him want to work harder. And his work ethic is off the charts. And and I got I I remember I took some um criticism for comparing his will and his mental toughness to Kobe Bryant but I think it's up there. Um is he as as talented as Kobe Bryant? No, but I think Kobe Bryant would be the first one, God rest his soul, to say, "Boy, um that's what I'm talking about." and point to Jalen Brunson. >> I mean, again, you you've been calling Knicks games forever and a day and um and I you know, I know you got to play it down the middle and you're you're such a pro. You're so good at what you do, Mike. Um but I'm wondering who are you thinking about from your early days on a day like today? Who are you you know, reminiscing with or or thinking about? >> Mike. >> There's been a lot and and that's part of the fun is is all the texts. I think when I got back to my hotel room that night, I I I probably had about 400 texts. And most of them were were Nick fans. Obviously, a lot of friends, co-workers, etc. Um but a lot of them were Nick fans. And of course, I think one of the people of course I think of was my dad. My I was one of six boys so in in our house, sports was not an option. And we just loved whatever um whatever team that my dad rooted for. And my dad was a he was a Marine and a construction worker, a tough guy. And I always thought he was the strongest man in the in the world and I used to think that Dave DeBusschere was the second strongest. So, that's the influence that he had on me. >> Um so, that's who I think of. And really, quite honestly, uh Rich, it's been so much fun sharing it with my kids. Um they're all they're not kids anymore. They're young adults at 34, 33, and 29, two boys and a girl. And they just they just love the Knicks and they go to the games and, you know, they saw a lot of bad basketball growing up. So, for them uh to really enjoy it. My wife and my daughter are Villanova grads, so you can imagine how much uh they love the the the Nova Knicks. Um so, that's that's And that's what we said earlier. It's it's sharing with so many people uh the joy of them coming together like this and especially a team like this that carries themselves like this, that play like this. >> Have you connected with Clyde? >> Well, yeah, I saw him I saw him after the game. >> that like? >> Um it was it was so wonderful. He he's my friendship with Clyde is one of the blessings of my life and he um I've never heard him talk about any other Nick team with the kind of reverence he talks about this team. He doesn't compare anybody to the '70 '70 team especially, but the '70 and '73. He thinks this team reminds him of that. He doesn't compare anyone to Willis Reed. Willis Reed was his role model, was his idol till the day Willis passed away. And he says that Jalen Brunson reminds him of Willis Reed in terms of, you know, that that silent but tough leader. Um so, he was he was more emotional than I thought. Um and it's it was wonderful to see. Patrick Ewing was so emotional after the game. Uh and the Knicks have done a great job bringing him back and and making him a real part of of the team in terms of uh using his his counsel and and letting him talk to the players and letting him work with the players. And Patrick was was so emotional after the game and he says, "I'm finally getting my ring." I mean, how do you not get emotional that he said something like that? >> Mike, this photo that we have on the screen, if you wouldn't mind putting it up right there. I mean, I I I didn't shed a tear on Saturday night. I was just taking it all in cuz I was in such disbelief. This photograph where he's smiling cuz he's holding the Larry O'Brien trophy. Patrick Ewing gets to hold this trophy. And Brunson is standing next to him. And again, they've known each other, right? He's Patrick said he's known Brunson since he was two because he was teammates with Rick. And Brunson's face here is basically saying, "Yeah, I'm I'm I'm so proud that I could make this moment happen." That's the way I'm looking at it. I'm wondering how you take this photograph in. >> Yeah, it's um there's such respect there. And often there's a disconnect between the way the older players approach and today's players approach. And the game we know is so different. But a lot of the the most important parts are not different. And I think that that Clyde has has and he's talked about it on the air and he's talked about it off the air. He has such reverence uh for the way Jalen handles his business. And he's been so respectful to Clyde as well. I mean, I watched him so much. He's one of the reasons why I fell in love with with doing this as a profession. His influence on how I call a game, certainly not I don't have his iconic voice, but um the way I call a game, the way I approach the profession, so much for me. So, I hope that some of that there.
